content:
I've formalized both parts of https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01I9 (Lemma 26.7.3) — natural isomorphisms showing that the tilde functor M ↦ M̃ intertwines with pullback and pushforward along morphisms of affine schemes, up to extension/restriction of scalars. These lemmas open up one route to fpqc descent in mathlib. These were fully generated with custom AI tooling (as well as part of this post). These are two stacked PRs:

PR 1 — PullbackTilde:
For f : R ⟶ S and ψ = Spec.map f: pullbackSpecTildeIso : tilde.functor R ⋙ pullback ψ ≅ extendScalars f ⋙ tilde.functor S

Proof: both sides are left adjoints of naturally isomorphic right adjoints, via Adjunction.leftAdjointUniq. The bridge is an auxiliary pushforwardΓRestrictScalarsIso identifying pushforward ψ ⋙ Γ_R ≅ Γ_S ⋙ restrictScalars f.

Branch: https://github.com/rdeager/mathlib4/tree/RE/pullback-tilde-iso

PR 2 — PushforwardTilde:
pushforwardSpecTildeIso : restrictScalars f ⋙ tilde.functor R ≅ tilde.functor S ⋙ pushforward ψ
Proof: construct the natural map as an adjunction transpose, then show each component is iso by proving ψ_*(Ñ) ∈ essImage(tilde_R). This uses an affine criterion (mem_essImage_tilde_of_basicOpen_localizations): a sheaf on Spec R is quasi-coherent iff its restriction maps to basic opens D(r) are localizations of global sections. The localization property is transferred from the S-module tilde through restrictScalars.

Branch: https://github.com/rdeager/mathlib4/tree/RE/pushforward-tilde-iso

Questions:

1. Is Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/Modules/ the right placement for these files?
2. Should I split IsLocalizedModule.isIso_of_factoring and the OrderTop instances into prerequisite PRs first?
3. Any suggestions for reducing the erw usage? Update: All ewrs eliminated.

Before you expect a mathlib expert to have a look at what your AI automatically generated, you should tell your AI to adapt the code to mathlib style, put lemmas in the right place, make the naming consistent with the library and the naming convention and work on removing all erws itself.

Finally, you should carefully review every single line of the code to verify that the mathematical strategy the agent is following is sensible and aligns with the references you are giving.

Note also that there are human mathematician/Lean experts who are working on very closely related results (with a non-trivial intersection with your content), and as a mathlib reviewer, I would certainly prioritize their pull requests.

Richard -- basically the community is well aware that AI can be used to write crappy-but-compiling code, but many contributors contributing AI-generated code (which is essentially never merged) seem to be unaware that PRing that crappy code to mathlib leads to a lot of wasted maintainer time patiently telling people who are trying to be helpful that their crappy code is nowhere near the standards which mathlib aspires to. Furthermore that if the user is not an expert then neither they nor the machine are in a position to fix it. This makes giving feedback to the AI users a thankless task, which is why the maintainers far prefer working with human experts, who typically write great code which is worth reviewing to make it even better so that all the humans learn and the library remains excellent.

This will change when either (a) AI gets good at writing excellent code (rather than crappy-but-compiling code) or (b) the community finds a place for AI-generated extensions of their library where AI code (which can be hell to maintain) can be dumped while the community figures out how to deal with this influx of new users using AI tools to generate Lean code; however this library will almost certainly not be mathlib itself, it will be more akin to a downstream "sloplib" was discussed at great length in #general a couple of months ago.

I agree that generating AI-generated proofs is the easy part and refactoring them up to mathlib standards is an interesting challenge. It would be helpful to give concrete references to other work formalizing [Stacks 01I9] or fpqc descent. I am aware of related work on Galois descent in https://github.com/chrisflav/pi1 and https://github.com/chrisflav/proetale. The first candidate PR at

https://github.com/rdeager/mathlib4/tree/RE/isLocalizedModule-isIso

is the following addition to

Algebra/Category/ModuleCat/Localization.lean

/-- A morphism in `ModuleCat` factoring between two `S`-localizations is an isomorphism. -/
lemma isIso_of_comp_eq {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {A B C : ModuleCat.{u} R}
    (S : Submonoid R) (g : A ⟶ B) (h : A ⟶ C)
    [IsLocalizedModule S g.hom] [IsLocalizedModule S h.hom]
    (α : B ⟶ C) (fac : α.hom ∘ₗ g.hom = h.hom) :
    IsIso α := by
  have hα : α = (IsLocalizedModule.linearEquiv S g.hom h.hom).toModuleIso.hom :=
    ModuleCat.hom_ext (eq_linearEquiv S g.hom h.hom α.hom fac)
  rw [hα]
  infer_instance

with helpers in Algebra/Module/LocalizedModule/Basic.lean. If helpful, I can split into two PRs.

Another issue with AI-generated proofs is that once some AI has produced crappy-but-compiling code for a certain result, it can be very discouraging for human contributors (especially those at an early stage of their careers) who would feel no incentive to make the effort of a clean formalisation work for mathlib as the outside world may just think they have only reimplemented an already existing proof.
Christian Merten and I have been formalising various formulations of what it means to be a stack #24434 (draft), and up to the equivalence between modules over a ring and quasi-coherent sheaves over the spectrum of this ring and a few other results, when all the pieces fit together, mathlib shall know that quasi-coherent sheaves over schemes form a fpqc stack, as this will reduce to the main result in https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/Category/ModuleCat/Descent.html
